answer: Effect size estimates tend to be larger in original studies compared to replication studies across all three disciplines (Social, Cognitive, Economics), indicating a general replication shrinkage pattern. The gap between original and replication effect sizes is largest in the Social and Cognitive domains, which are nearly on par in mean absolute gap (Social: 0.192, Cognitive: 0.190 on the correlation scale), but Social leads in the proportion of studies where the original effect exceeds the replication (88.2% vs 82.4%). The Economics domain shows a smaller gap (mean 0.169; 83.3% of studies), suggesting that experimental-economics effects are somewhat more robust to replication. Robustness checks on the Fisher-z scale, using relative_es < 1 as the criterion, and restricting to same-direction replications all confirm the same qualitative ranking: Social ≥ Cognitive > Economics in terms of original-vs-replication effect-size shrinkage. Thus, the domains in which effect sizes tend to be largest in original studies relative to replications are Social and Cognitive psychology, with Social showing the highest rate of shrinkage.

payload.workflow: 1) Inspection: loaded CSV (86×60), verified 0 NaN in key fields, 0 duplicate study IDs, confirmed ro always positive. 2) Primary comparison: computed |ro| vs |rr| gap and fraction per discipline (Cognitive, Social, Economics) on correlation scale. 3) Robustness checks: (a) Fisher-z scale (fiso vs |fisr|), (b) relative_es < 1 criterion, (c) excluding sign-reversed replications (rr<0), (d) project.x 2-level grouping, (e) median vs mean gap. 4) Data-quality note: row 41 (Eitam et al.) has a sign anomaly in relative_es (fisr>0 but relative_es<0); does not affect primary analysis. 5) Formulated natural-language hypothesis based on consistent pattern across all metrics.
